sections.body: Agent workflows in finance are the places where a language model or a small team of them is wired into a real desk process rather than a demo. The work is document heavy and repetitive: a request for proposal arrives and someone has to answer it, two counterparties haggle over terms for an over the counter trade, an investment committee needs a memo, a comparable company set drifts out of date, a trade has to settle. What the agents actually do now is read the incoming material, pull the relevant figures from internal systems and prior documents, draft a first pass, and route it to a human for sign off. The interesting part is not the writing, it is the retrieval and the checking against source records, because a fluent paragraph with a wrong number is worse than no paragraph at all.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The drafting side is the most mature, since proposal responses and committee memos are largely assembly of known facts into a known structure, and models are good at that when they are given the right inputs. Negotiation is the least settled, because an agent has to hold a position over multiple rounds, infer what the other side will accept, and know when it lacks authority to concede anything. Settlement automation sits in the middle, technically tractable but constrained by legacy formats, matching rules and the fact that a failed settlement is expensive and visible. The honest limits are consistent across all of it: agents cannot be trusted with numbers they have not been given, they degrade when source documents conflict, and every workflow here still needs a named human who owns the output. Nothing in this section is advice, and none of it removes the compliance and counterparty obligations that sit with the firm.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages run roughly in the order a deal moves. Drafting Proposal Responses covers the front end, where an incoming request is parsed and a structured answer is produced, and it is the natural starting point for anyone new to the area. Agent Negotiation in Over the Counter Markets takes on the hardest case, where the agent is not summarising but acting over several turns, and it is where the open questions live. Investment Committee Memos is the internal counterpart, turning analysis into a document a committee can argue with, while Keeping Comparable Company Sets Current handles the quieter problem of keeping the underlying reference data from going stale. Automating Trade Settlement closes the loop on the post trade side, and a reader who wants to see how far the same techniques stretch from drafting to execution should read it last.
